item.title: Resolving Tomcat JDBC Driver Memory Leak Warnings with ServiceLoader Registration
item.description:
“Resolving Tomcat JDBC Driver Memory Leak Warnings with ServiceLoader Registration”

Encountering warnings related to JDBC driver memory leaks during Tomcat shutdown, often stemming from drivers auto-registering via the ServiceLoader API, is a common hurdle in servlet container environments. While Tomcat 6.0.24+ attempts to prevent actual memory leaks, these informational messages point to underlying issues in the driver’s lifecycle management. How should developers address these alerts effectively?

The Root Cause: Auto-Registration Without Manual Deregistration

The core issue arises when a JDBC 4.0 compatible driver residing in the web application’s /WEB-INF/lib directory automatically registers itself during application startup using ServiceLoader. Upon web application shutdown, this driver fails to de-register itself, triggering a warning from Tomcat’s leak detection mechanism.

item.title: Java Tomcat UTF-8 Encoding Issues Explained and Solved
item.description:
“Java Tomcat UTF-8 Encoding Issues Explained and Solved”

Encountering issues with special characters like äåö or Cyrillic letters when using Java, Tomcat, and MySQL? This post delves into common UTF-8 encoding problems and provides a series of solutions contributed by developers who have navigated these challenges. We’ll cover server configurations, Java code adjustments, database settings, and browser behavior to ensure your web applications handle international characters correctly.

The Challenge: Character Encoding Mismatches

The core of the problem often lies in inconsistencies in character encoding across different components of a web application stack. While many systems default to Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), proper handling of a wider range of characters requires a consistent UTF-8 implementation. This can affect GET and POST requests, responses, JSP pages, and even database connections.

item.title: what is Apache tomcat detault username and password?
item.description:
Summary

Tomcat is one of the most popular Java-based web servers, but its default configurations might leave it vulnerable if not properly secured. One of the most crucial aspects of securing Tomcat is configuring user roles and setting strong Apache tomcat detault username and password. In this guide, we’ll walk through five essential methods to secure your Tomcat installation by managing user access and customizing roles, using practical examples, unique code snippets, and step-by-step explanations.
